sourcedFrom: NOMAD  OWNER'S MANUAL — Rev121323 (UNKNOWN — not printed in the document; the revision stamp reads Rev121323)
cleanIntro: The Nomad L is the long Nomad: a fully-welded 17-4 PH stainless .30 can with a modular back cap that takes either a direct-thread adapter or a Key-Mo fast-attach mount, and a front cap that unscrews for a cap change. Dead Air's book for it is the Nomad series owner's manual, and that book teaches mounting, unmounting and thread care — it publishes no procedure for opening the tube, and none is invented here. One caution to read before you start: the caliber-ceiling sentence in this book is written naming the Nomad-30, so the markings on your own can and its packaging are what govern, exactly as that sentence itself says.

steps.title: Clear the host — and use the host's own manual to do it
steps.action: Before the can is touched, drop the magazine, lock the action open and both look and feel into the chamber. Dead Air is explicit that clearing procedure belongs to the firearm's book, not to this one, and that the suppressor never goes on or comes off a closed action.
steps.prose: A suppressor manual can only speak for the can. If there is any doubt about how your rifle unloads, that answer lives in the rifle's manual.
steps.quote: CHECK YOUR WEAPON’S CHAMBER AND MAKE CERTAIN THAT THE WEAPON IS UNLOADED AND THE MAGAZINE REMOVED BEFORE PROCEEDING ANY FURTHER. IF THERE IS ANY QUESTION OR DOUBT, CONSULT THE OPERATOR’S MANUAL APPLICABLE TO YOUR FIREARM AS TO THE PROPER PROCEDURE FOR CLEARING AND/OR UNLOADING YOUR WEAPON. DO NOT INSTALL YOUR NEW SUPPRESSOR ON A FIREARM WITH A CLOSED ACTION!
steps.cite: NOMAD  OWNER'S MANUAL — Rev121323 — Product Overview — General Considerations, printed pp.4–5 (2-up spread)
steps.warn: Never fit or remove this suppressor on a firearm with a closed action.

steps.title: The pressure ceiling — and whose name is on it
steps.action: Read the ceiling before you read anything else, and read it carefully. This is the Nomad series book, and the sentence that states the pressure limit is written naming the Nomad-30. It also names the thing that overrides it: what is engraved on the suppressor itself and printed on the packaging. Check the markings on your own Nomad L and treat those as the statement of what your unit is rated for.
steps.prose: Sub-calibres are explicitly fine — the manual names 5.56 as acceptable. It is the top end that is bounded, and the boundary is a chamber pressure, not a bullet diameter.
steps.quote: OUR PRODUCTS ARE CALIBER SPECIFIC. UNLESS STATED OTHERWISE ON THE SUPPRESSOR ITSELF OR ON THE PACKAGING, THE NOMAD-30 SUPPRESSOR WILL NOT FUNCTION SAFELY WITH ANY CARTRIDGE WITH PRESSURES HIGHER THAN 300 WINMAG. SUB-CALIBERS LIKE 5.56 ARE ACCEPTABLE.
steps.cite: NOMAD  OWNER'S MANUAL — Rev121323 — Silencer Installation and Removal — Step One: Preparation, printed p.9
steps.warn: This ceiling sentence names the Nomad-30. The engraving on your own can and its packaging override it — the sentence says so itself.

steps.title: Ammunition and thread concentricity decide whether it survives
steps.action: Two things outside the can govern how it fares. Use good quality factory-new ammunition, and satisfy yourself that the muzzle threads on your barrel are cut concentric with the bore. If you have no way to check concentricity, Dead Air's own advice is to have a competent gunsmith check it rather than find out by baffle strike.
steps.prose: A can that suddenly shoots badly, or shows a bright strike mark inside the front cap, is almost always telling you about the threads it is hanging on.
steps.aside: The same section reads: "Ammunition:  Ammunition will have a huge influence on how your new suppressor functions. Use good quality factory-new ammunition in your firearm."
steps.quote: Concentricity: In order to reduce the risk of a baffle strike, it is important to ensure that your barrel threads are aligned concentrically with the bore axis of your host weapon’s barrel.
steps.cite: NOMAD  OWNER'S MANUAL — Rev121323 — Product Overview — General Considerations, printed pp.4–5 (2-up spread)

steps.title: Know which back cap you are running before you turn anything
steps.action: Identify your mount first. The Nomad's back cap accepts either a direct-thread adapter that screws straight onto your barrel, or a Key-Mo fast-attach mount that locks onto a Key-Mount brake or flash hider. The two come off the host in different ways, so establish which one is fitted before you start turning the tube.
steps.prose: The front cap is modular too — it takes the Dead Air cap inserts and the E-brake — which is why a cap change is a normal owner job on this can and opening the body is not.
steps.quote: Back cap is designed for direct thread or Key-Mo fast-attach mounts. Front cap takes all Sandman cap inserts and E-brake
steps.cite: NOMAD  OWNER'S MANUAL — Rev121323 — Product Overview — Key Features, printed p.4

steps.title: Direct thread: unscrew the body off the muzzle
steps.action: With a direct-thread adapter installed, take the whole suppressor off by rotating the body counter-clockwise until it starts to unthread from the muzzle. Check the thread hand first — some barrel threads are left-handed, and on those you unscrew clockwise instead.
steps.prose: If the body unthreads but leaves the adapter behind on the barrel, that is a loose adapter, not a fault: the hook spanner is what takes the adapter off.
steps.quote: To remove the suppressor when the Direct Thread Adapter is installed, simply rotate the body of the suppressor counter-clockwise until it begins to unthread from the muzzle of the host weapon. If the thread is left-handed, then unscrew by rotating clockwise.
steps.cite: NOMAD  OWNER'S MANUAL — Rev121323 — Silencer Installation and Removal — Step Three: Removing the Suppressor, printed p.10
steps.warn: WARNING! THE SUPPRESSOR MAY BECOME EXTREMELY HOT AFTER USE. NEVER GRAB A HOT SUPPRESSOR AS IT CAN RESULT IN BURNS AND INJURY.

steps.title: Key-Mo: three-quarters of a turn and it lifts off
steps.action: With a Key-Mo adapter installed the can does not unthread — rotate the body counter-clockwise about three-quarters of a turn until it stops turning, then slide it straight off the brake or flash hider. Left in that state it is already indexed for the next time it goes on.
steps.prose: The stop is positive. If it keeps turning past three-quarters of a turn you are unthreading the adapter out of the can rather than releasing it from the brake.
steps.aside: The manual also notes: "If the suppressor unthreads from the mount with the mount remaining on the barrel, then the Hook Spanner can be used to loosen it."
steps.quote: The suppressor may now be slipped off the brake or flash hider. In this state, it’s ready for re-installation upon its next use.
steps.cite: NOMAD  OWNER'S MANUAL — Rev121323 — Silencer Installation and Removal — Step Three: Removing the Suppressor, printed p.10

steps.title: Adapter out of the can — two hook spanners, opposite directions
steps.action: To change the mount adapter, catch the notches in the adapter and in the suppressor with the two hook spanner wrenches so that the adapter turns counter-clockwise while the suppressor turns clockwise. Set the hooks an inch or two apart so you can squeeze them together for leverage, then keep loosening and draw the adapter out of the back of the can.
steps.prose: Both hands work against each other here. Trying it with one wrench and a hand on the tube just twists the tube.
steps.quote: Use the Hook Spanners to catch the notches in the parts such that the mount is being turned Counter-Clockwise and the suppressor Clockwise.
steps.cite: NOMAD  OWNER'S MANUAL — Rev121323 — Mount Removal — Step One, printed p.7
steps.warn: WHEN THE TORQUE BREAKS BETWEEN THE TWO PARTS, THE WRENCHES MAY SWING ENOUGH TO CREATE A PINCH POINT. ALWAYS BE CAREFUL AND MIND THE GAP!

steps.title: If it will not break loose, heat it — and mind the heat
steps.action: A mount that has been through heavy heat cycles, or that was fitted with a high-strength thread locker, may not come free cold. Dead Air's published remedy is heat: warm the suppressor to loosen the threads, and keep track of which surfaces you have just made hot enough to burn you.
steps.prose: This is the opposite of the Nomad Ti OTB's rule, where Rocksett is involved and heat is expressly ruled out. Read the book for the can in your hand.
steps.caution: Heat makes every surface on the can dangerous, not just the joint you were aiming at.
steps.quote: YOU MAY NEED TO HEAT THE SUPPRESSOR UP TO LOOSEN THE THREADS. PAY SPECIAL ATTENTION TO THE HEATED SURFACES TO AVOID BURNS!
steps.cite: NOMAD  OWNER'S MANUAL — Rev121323 — Mount Removal, printed p.7

steps.title: Front cap off with the pin tool, never with pliers
steps.action: The front cap comes off with a pin tool, not by gripping it. Align the pins of the Sandman Front Cap Tool into the holes cut in the cap, make sure the tool sits flat with every pin fully home, and turn counter-clockwise to loosen. A tool that is cocked or only half engaged will round out the holes.
steps.prose: The tool is DA203 and is sold separately. That is the whole of the front-cap procedure this book publishes.
steps.quote: Align the pins in the Sandman Front Cap Tool (DA203—sold separately) into the holes cut into the front cap. Ensure tool is flat against the front cap with the pins evenly and fully engaged and apply torque Counter-Clockwise to loosen and remove.
steps.cite: NOMAD  OWNER'S MANUAL — Rev121323 — Front Cap Installation and Removal — Step One, printed p.8

steps.title: Threads and taper — clean, then grease
steps.action: Clean the threads and the taper on both parts before anything goes back together, then put high-quality grease on those surfaces. This is the maintenance the Nomad book actually publishes: the mating surfaces, not the inside of the tube.
steps.prose: Grease on the adapter threads is also what keeps a mount from seizing after a hot string, which is what turns a two-minute job into a heat-gun job.
steps.quote: Clean threads and taper. Apply high quality grease to the surfaces and install new cap and hand tighten.
steps.cite: NOMAD  OWNER'S MANUAL — Rev121323 — Front Cap Installation and Removal — Step Two, printed p.8

steps.title: Debris on a thread or a taper is a baffle strike waiting to happen
steps.action: Before reassembly, look at what you are about to close up. Grit on a thread or on a taper does not just make the joint tight — it holds the parts out of alignment, and on a suppressor that misalignment puts the bullet into a baffle or the front cap. Clean both mating parts and tighten again rather than forcing a component that will not seat.
steps.prose: The tell is a component that will not go fully snug. That is the manual's own trigger for stopping and inspecting.
steps.quote: NOTE: DEBRIS ON THE THREADS AND TAPER SURFACES MAY CAUSE MISALIGNMENT OF SUPPRESSOR PARTS AND ALLOW FOR BULLET STRIKES ON BAFFLES OR THE FRONT CAP.
steps.cite: NOMAD  OWNER'S MANUAL — Rev121323 — Silencer Installation and Removal — Step Four: Inspection Upon Assembly, printed p.11
steps.warn: Debris on a thread or taper can put a bullet into your baffles.

steps.title: Barrel threads clean and lubed before it goes back on
steps.action: Clean and lubricate the host's muzzle threads before the can goes back, and start it carefully by hand. If it does not thread on smoothly, stop — do not force it and do not reach for a wrench; a suppressor that will not start cleanly is telling you something about the threads.
steps.prose: The can must end up tight against the shoulder of the barrel. On a long thread it may seat on the muzzle face instead, with the back of the adapter clear of the shoulder — that is normal on those barrels.
steps.caution: Never thread this can onto a barrel with no proper shoulder or a muzzle face that is not square with the bore.
steps.quote: Before installation, ensure the threads of the host firearm’s barrel are clean and lubed before carefully threading the suppressor onto the muzzle end of your firearm.
steps.cite: NOMAD  OWNER'S MANUAL — Rev121323 — Silencer Installation and Removal — Step One: Preparation, printed p.9

steps.title: Field strip complete
steps.action: The Nomad L is off the host, the mount adapter is either still in the can or out of it on the bench, and the front cap is off if you were changing it. That is the whole of the strip this book publishes. The tube itself is a fully-welded assembly and there is no owner procedure for opening it.
steps.prose: Everything from here is threads, tapers, grease and torque — which is exactly where a .30 can wins or loses its accuracy.
steps.quote: The Nomad-30 is made with 17-4 Stainless Steel and Grade 5 titanium.
steps.cite: NOMAD  OWNER'S MANUAL — Rev121323 — Product Overview, printed p.4

deepAbsentReason: The Nomad series owner's manual publishes NO cleaning or disassembly procedure at all. Its table of contents is Product Overview, Get To Know Your Nomad-30, Mount Installation, Mount Removal, Front Cap Installation and Removal, Silencer Installation and Removal, Disclaimer, Warranty, Lawful Use and Possession, Contact Information — there is no cleaning section, no solvent guidance, no baffle or tube procedure and no service interval anywhere in the nine pages. The only cleaning the book states is of the mating surfaces: "Clean threads and taper", "Clean both mating parts as necessary", and the barrel threads "clean and lubed" before installation. The tube is a welded assembly. Searched and re-confirmed against the maker's live site on 2026-08-20: /silencers/nomad-l/ publishes exactly two documents, this manual and the Fitment Guide Booklet, and no deeper procedure exists to cite. Nothing beyond what the book prints has been invented. The manual's own direction for anything further is: "Any questions concerning the performance or care of your suppressor should be directed to our Customer Service Department (801) 857-4232."

cleaning.name: MOUNT ADAPTER & BACK CAP THREADS
tasks: Clean the adapter threads and the suppressor's rear threads whenever the mount is changed
Coat the threads with a high-quality grease before the adapter goes back in
Where heavy heat cycles have been loosening the mount, degrease instead and use a medium-strength high-temperature thread locker
Check the adapter is bottomed out on the rear suppressor face

cleaning.name: FRONT CAP & TAPER
tasks: Clean the cap threads and the taper, then grease both surfaces
Use the pin tool squarely — every pin fully engaged, tool flat against the cap
Hand tighten the cap; there is no published torque figure for it
Inspect the cap bore for strike marks whenever the can has been on a new host

cleaning.name: HOST MUZZLE THREADS
tasks: Clean and lube the barrel threads before every installation
Confirm the can seats fully against the barrel shoulder, or on the muzzle face where the thread is long
Re-check tightness often — a direct-thread can loosens with use
Never fit it to a barrel with no proper shoulder, or a muzzle face out of square with the bore

cleaning.name: INSPECTION
tasks: Every component snug, with no gaps and no rattle
Anything not fully tight: check the threads for damage or debris, clean and repeat
Look down the bore path for a strike mark on a baffle or the front cap
Let the can reach ambient temperature before handling it bare-handed

reassembly: Choose the mount adapter for your host and coat its threads with high-quality grease.
Thread the adapter into the back of the suppressor until it bottoms out on the rear suppressor face.
Set the two hook spanners an inch or two apart on the notches and turn the adapter clockwise against the suppressor counter-clockwise to tighten.
If the front cap was removed, clean and grease the threads and taper, install the cap and hand tighten it.
Clean and lube the host's barrel threads, then start the suppressor on by hand — hand tightening is preferred; the hook spanner adds only a little more if needed.
Seat it fully against the barrel shoulder, and keep Key-Mount muzzle devices and direct-thread adapters at 20–25 ft-lbs on the barrel, never above 30.
fncheck: With the can mounted, look down the bore path against the light and confirm it is straight, centred and clear. Then visually check the suppressor is square to the centreline of the bore and not canted, and that every component is snug with no gaps or rattle. If it is not in line with the bore, or anything rattles, it does not get fired — stop and contact Dead Air. Re-check tightness often once you are shooting: a direct-thread can loosens with use, and a loose can shifts the point of impact and can strike a baffle.
